title: Italian grammar
about: From your very first conversation to everyday fluency, one short lesson at a time. Each lesson gives you something you can say straight away, then the grammar that makes it work. You don't need to know any grammar: each grammar word is explained when you first need it. Every example is the Italian spoken in Italy today, with its accents written as they should be.

lessons.title: Say hello and who you are
lessons.summary: Greet someone, say your name and where you're from, and ask them the same: your first Italian conversation.
lessons.topic: {{sono, sei, è}} (“I am, you are, he/she is”), with no word for “I”; {{mi chiamo}}; {{di}} + a city

goal.t: Ciao, sono Anna. Sono di Londra.
goal.tr: Hi, I'm Anna. I'm from London.

dialog.tr: I'm from Rome. Nice to meet you!

blocks.p: **I am, you are.** {{sono}} means “I am” and {{sei}} “you are” (to a friend). Notice that Anna often doesn't say a word for “I”: {{sono di Londra}} is, word for word, “am from London”. The verb itself already says who.

blocks.means: a word for doing or being: am, live, eat, go.
a short word that stands for a person or a thing: I, you, he, she.

table: {{io}} “I” only to stress it: {{Io sono di Roma}} “I'm from Rome (and you aren't)”
to a friend, a child, a relative

blocks.p: **Your name.** {{Sono Anna}} or {{Mi chiamo Anna}}, word for word “I call myself Anna”. To ask a friend: {{Come ti chiami?}} “What's your name?”

**Where you're from.** {{di}} + a city: {{Sono di Roma}}. For a country, say your nationality: {{Sono inglese}}, {{Sono americano}} (said by a man), {{Sono americana}} (said by a woman). Italian writes nationalities with a small letter.

ex.note: a question just by raising your voice at the end

ex.t: Lui è Paolo. È di Napoli.
ex.tr: This is Paolo. He's from Naples.

blocks.tip: The accent matters: {{è}} “is” and {{e}} “and” are two different words. Italian accents are part of the spelling, like the dot on an i.

mistakes.why: With {{sono}}, “from” is {{di}}. ({{da}} goes with {{vengo}} “I come”: {{Vengo da Londra}}.)
“Is” is {{è}}, with its accent; {{e}} without it means “and”.

practice.q: You want to say “I'm from Rome”. Which one?
practice.why: {{sono}} is “I am”; {{sei}} is “you are” and {{è}} “he or she is”.

practice.q: Choose the missing word.
You're Tom, from New York. Choose your replies.

options: Sono di New York. E tu?
Sei di New York. E tu?
lines.why: {{sono}} about yourself; {{E tu?}} “and you?” turns the question back.

lines.tr: I'm from Florence. Nice to meet you!

lines.why: {{Piacere mio!}}, “the pleasure is mine”, is the natural answer to {{Piacere!}}

practice.q: Put the words in order.
Ask a friend: “What's your name?”
Your turn: say hello, your name and where you're from. Start with {{Ciao, sono…}}

answers.t: Ciao, sono Emma. Sono di Toronto.
answers.tr: Hi, I'm Emma. I'm from Toronto.

answers.t: Ciao, mi chiamo James. Sono inglese, di Manchester.
answers.tr: Hi, my name is James. I'm English, from Manchester.

lessons.title: Greet people, casually or politely
lessons.summary: Say hello, ask how someone is and say goodbye, to a friend and to a stranger: the two Italian ways of saying “you”.

goal.tr: Good morning, Mrs. Rossi! How are you?

dialog.tr: Good morning, Mr. Bianchi. How are you?
Very well, thank you. And you?

blocks.p: **Two ways to say “you”.** Italian has a casual “you”, {{tu}}, for friends, family, children and people your age in relaxed places, and a polite one, {{Lei}}, for strangers, older people, shop and hotel staff, and anyone you'd call Mr. or Mrs. {{Lei}} takes the same verb as “she”: {{Come sta?}} is, word for word, “How is she?”, and it means “How are you?” said politely.
**“How are you” uses {{stare}}**, not {{essere}}: {{stai}} for {{tu}}, {{sta}} for {{Lei}}, and the answer {{sto bene}} “I'm fine”, or simply {{bene}}.

blocks.tip: When in doubt, start with {{Lei}}. If the other person prefers {{tu}}, they'll say so: {{Diamoci del tu!}} “Let's use tu!”. Young people use {{tu}} with each other straight away. {{Lei}} is often written with a capital L, to tell it apart from {{lei}} “she”.

mistakes.tr: Good morning, madam. How are you?
mistakes.why: To a stranger or an older person, use the polite {{sta}} ({{Lei}}), not {{stai}}.
“I'm fine” uses {{stare}}: {{sto bene}}. {{Sono bene}} isn't Italian.

practice.q: You meet your friend's grandmother for the first time. You say…
practice.why: A stranger and an older person: {{buongiorno}}, and the polite {{sta}}.

practice.q: Choose the missing word.
At the hotel desk, in the morning. Choose your replies.

lines.why: The receptionist is using {{Lei}}: answer the same way.
{{Arrivederci}} is the polite goodbye. ({{Ciao, bello!}} is “Bye, gorgeous!”)

practice.q: Put the words in order.
Say to a new friend: “Hi, I'm Ben. I'm from Boston.”
practice.answer: Ciao, sono Ben. Sono di Boston.

practice.q: Your turn: greet your neighbor, Mrs. Bianchi, and ask how she is; then greet a friend and ask the same.

answers.tr: Good morning, Mrs. Bianchi! How are you?

lessons.title: Order at the café
lessons.summary: Ask for a coffee, a pastry or a drink, politely: “I'd like a cappuccino, please.”
lessons.topic: {{vorrei}} “I'd like”; masculine and feminine nouns; “a”: {{un, uno, una, un'}}

goal.t: Vorrei un cappuccino e una spremuta, per favore.
goal.tr: I'd like a cappuccino and a fresh orange juice, please.

dialog.tr: Good morning! What will you have?

dialog.t: Vorrei un cappuccino e un cornetto, per favore.
dialog.tr: I'd like a cappuccino and a croissant, please.
Yes, a small bottle of water.

blocks.p: **{{Vorrei}}** is the polite “I'd like”: the word to use in a café, a shop or a hotel. Put what you want after it: {{vorrei un caffè}}. Add {{per favore}} “please”.

blocks.means: a word for a person, a thing, an animal or a place: coffee, girl, dog, Rome.
in Italian every noun is either masculine or feminine, even the names of things. It's a fact about the word, not the thing: {{tavolo}} “table” is masculine, {{sedia}} “chair” is feminine.

blocks.p: **Masculine or feminine?** The ending usually tells you: most nouns ending in {{-o}} are masculine ({{cornetto}}, {{panino}}), most ending in {{-a}} are feminine ({{pizza}}, {{birra}}). Nouns ending in {{-e}} can be either ({{latte}} “milk” is masculine, {{notte}} “night” feminine), and a few are simply worth learning ({{caffè}} and {{tè}} are masculine).
**“A” changes with the noun.** Italian has four forms of “a”, chosen by the noun's gender and its first sound:

table: masculine nouns starting with s + consonant, or z
feminine nouns starting with a vowel

ex.tr: I'd like a sandwich and a water.

blocks.tip: In Italy, {{un caffè}} is an espresso. Want a little milk in it? Ask for {{un caffè macchiato}}. And be careful: {{un latte}} is just a glass of milk!

mistakes.why: {{caffè}} is masculine, even though it doesn't end in -o: {{un}}.
{{acqua}} is feminine: {{una}}, which becomes {{un'}} (with an apostrophe) before a vowel. A masculine noun has no apostrophe: {{un amico}}.
{{voglio}} “I want” is correct Italian, but it sounds blunt when you order. {{vorrei}} is the polite way.

practice.q: Which “a” goes with {{birra}} “beer”?
Choose the missing word.
practice.tr: I'd like a fresh orange juice, please.

practice.q: Choose the missing word.
practice.why: A masculine noun starting with s + consonant: {{uno}}.

lines.tr: Good evening! What will you have?

lines.why: {{vorrei}} for what you want. ({{Sono uno spritz}} would be “I am a spritz”!)

practice.q: Put the words in order.

practice.q: Your turn: order your favorite breakfast or drink in an Italian café. Start with {{Vorrei…}}

answers.t: Vorrei un caffè macchiato e un cornetto, per favore.
answers.tr: I'd like an espresso with a dash of milk and a croissant, please.

answers.t: Vorrei un tè e una spremuta, per favore.
answers.tr: I'd like a tea and a fresh orange juice, please.

lessons.title: Say where you live and what you do
lessons.summary: Tell someone where you live, what languages you speak and where you work or study: your first verbs.
lessons.topic: The present of -are verbs ({{parlo, parli, parla…}}); the ending says who

goal.t: Abito a Londra e lavoro in banca.
goal.tr: I live in London and I work in a bank.

dialog.t: Adesso abito a Bologna. E tu?
dialog.tr: I live in Bologna now. And you?
Me too. Do you work here?

dialog.t: Sì, lavoro in un ristorante. E studio italiano!
dialog.tr: Yes, I work in a restaurant. And I'm studying Italian!

blocks.means: the basic form of a verb, the one in the dictionary: to live, to work. In Italian it ends in -are, -ere or -ire: {{parlare}} “to speak”, {{prendere}} “to take”, {{dormire}} “to sleep”.

blocks.p: **The ending says who.** To use a verb, take off {{-are}} and add the ending for the person. Most verbs ending in {{-are}} work exactly like these two:

blocks.means: who or what does the action of the verb: in “Anna works”, Anna is the subject.

blocks.p: Because the ending says who the subject is, Italians usually leave out {{io}} “I”, {{tu}} “you” and the rest: {{Parlo inglese}} “I speak English”. Say them only to stress or to contrast: {{Io lavoro, e tu?}} “I work, and you?”

**One present for two.** {{lavoro}} is both “I work” and “I'm working”, {{studio italiano}} both “I study Italian” and “I'm studying Italian”. And a question needs no “do”: {{Lavori qui?}} “Do you work here?”

ex.t: Parlo inglese e un po' di italiano.
ex.tr: I speak English and a little Italian.

blocks.tip: Living in a city: {{a}}; in a country: {{in}}. {{Abito a Milano, in Italia}} “I live in Milan, in Italy”.

mistakes.why: Use the verb with its ending ({{abito}}), not the dictionary form; and {{io}} isn't needed.
For he or she, the ending is {{-a}}: {{lavora}}. {{lavoro}} means “I work”.

practice.q: Choose the missing word.
{{Parliamo italiano}} means…
Choose the missing word.
Meeting someone in your building: choose your replies.

lines.why: The verb takes the ending for “I”: {{abito}}.
{{studio}} is “I study”; {{studia}} is “he or she studies”.

practice.q: Put the words in order.
practice.tr: We live in Rome, but we work in Florence.

practice.q: Say: “I'm from Chicago, but I live in Rome.”
practice.answer: Sono di Chicago, ma abito a Roma.

practice.q: Your turn: where do you live, what languages do you speak, where do you work or study? Use {{abito}}, {{parlo}}, {{lavoro}} or {{studio}}.

answers.t: Abito a Boston e lavoro in un ospedale.
answers.tr: I live in Boston and I work in a hospital.

answers.t: Abito a Sydney. Parlo inglese e studio italiano.
answers.tr: I live in Sydney. I speak English and I'm studying Italian.

lessons.title: Get to know someone
lessons.summary: Ask where someone is from, where they live, what they do and why they're here, to a friend or politely.
lessons.topic: Questions: the voice going up, and the question words {{chi, cosa, dove, quando, come, perché, quanto}}

goal.t: Di dove sei? E che lavoro fai?
goal.tr: Where are you from? And what do you do for a living?

dialog.tr: And why are you in Italy?

dialog.t: Studio italiano a Siena. Tu che lavoro fai?
dialog.tr: I'm studying Italian in Siena. What do you do?

blocks.p: **Yes-or-no questions** look exactly like statements: only your voice changes, going up at the end. {{Parli inglese.}} “You speak English.” {{Parli inglese?}} “Do you speak English?” There is no word for “do”.

table: {{Perché studi italiano?}} “Why are you studying Italian?”

blocks.p: {{perché}} means both “why?” and “because”: {{Perché studi italiano? Perché amo l'Italia!}} “Why are you studying Italian? Because I love Italy!”

**To someone you call {{Lei}}**, the verb takes the “he, she” ending: {{Di dov'è?}} “Where are you from?”, {{Dove abita?}} “Where do you live?”, {{Che lavoro fa?}} “What do you do?” ({{fai}} and {{fa}} come from {{fare}} “to do, to make”, a verb you'll meet again.)

ex.note: polite: {{è}} for “you are”; {{dov'è}} is {{dove è}} run together
polite; to a friend, {{Come ti chiami?}}

ex.tr: What do you do? I'm a doctor.
ex.note: after {{sono}}, a job usually has no “a”

blocks.tip: A question that needs “from” starts with it: {{Di dove sei?}} is, word for word, “Of where are you?”. Italian never leaves a little word like {{di}} at the end of a question.

mistakes.why: The little word {{di}} goes at the start of the question, with {{dove}}.
{{perché}} needs its accent: é, sloping up to the right.

practice.q: How do you ask a friend “Do you speak English?”
practice.why: There's no word for “do”: say the sentence and let your voice go up.

practice.q: Choose the missing word.
practice.tr: Where do you live? In Naples.

practice.q: Choose the missing word.
practice.tr: Where are you from, Mr. Bianchi?
practice.why: You're being polite to Mr. Bianchi ({{Lei}}): {{è}}.
